title: Genre-Based Writing — The Teaching Cycle

pts: Building the field, deconstruction, joint construction, and independent construction form the cycle's four stages.
Each stage systematically reduces teacher support as learner control over the genre increases.
This structured scaffolding-and-release approach is far more reliable than 'read examples, then write your own.'
points.who: The Sydney School's genre-based pedagogy (Rothery, Martin)

blocks.x: Most time goes to the last stage, which is the one learners are least prepared for. The cycle redistributes time so that support is gradually reduced (Rothery 1994; Martin and Rose 2008).

body: The Sydney School’s genre work began in schools serving disadvantaged communities. Its founders argued that leaving learners to discover school genres by themselves favours those who already meet them at home, and that making genres explicit is a matter of fairness as well as method (Martin and Rose 2008).

pts: Before analysing genre structure, ensure learners have the content knowledge the genre will need to convey.
A learner who doesn't understand the topic cannot produce a strong genre example regardless of structural teaching.
This connects to Unit 37's CLIL principle that content and language demands are often intertwined.

v: Four stations with pictures, data, short readings and interview questions

items: Announce the genre and topic, for example a discussion text on whether a town should build a new flyover.
Set up four stations: photographs, a traffic table, a short news report and a set of interview questions.
Groups rotate every eight minutes, noting facts and viewpoints in a shared chart.
For homework, learners interview one family member or neighbour, in any language, and note the answers in English.
Build a class word bank of topic vocabulary.
Invite a guest speaker, such as a traffic police officer or a local shopkeeper.
Support: provide a note-taking grid with headings.
Challenge: learners find one statistic from a reliable source to add to the class chart.

blocks.x: A class chart after the carousel (written for this book):

lines: For: less traffic at the junction; faster ambulances; less pollution from idling vehicles.
Against: trees cut down; shops below lose customers; traffic may shift to the next junction.
S1: My uncle said, in Telugu, that his shop lost business when the last flyover was built.
T: That’s valuable evidence. How would you say it in English for our chart?

blocks.x: A learner who does not understand the topic cannot write a strong example of the genre, however well the structure is taught. This is the CLIL principle of Unit 37: content and language demands are intertwined.

body: Purpose: to show field-building as preparation. Content: a well being filled with buckets labelled ‘pictures’, ‘data’, ‘reading’ and ‘interviews’, before a learner draws water from it to write. Style: rural Indian setting, warm colours. Board version: a well drawn as a circle with four arrows into it.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for a shared class chart of facts and views.

blocks.x: Chart paper on the wall; groups add notes with sketch pens.

pts: Analyse a model text's genre structure and moves explicitly, extending Unit 33's move analysis into a full teaching stage.
Multiple models at this stage reveal which structural features are fixed conventions versus flexible choices.
This stage should be genuinely analytical, not just a passive reading of an example.

v: Three short discussion texts on different topics

items: Give groups three short discussion texts.
Groups label the stages in each: issue, arguments for, arguments against, recommendation.
Groups identify language features in each stage, such as connectors of contrast, hedged claims and modal verbs in the recommendation.
Compare the three texts: which features are fixed conventions and which are choices?
Build a class chart of stages and features.
Include one weak model and ask what makes it weaker.
Support: provide stage labels to match to paragraphs.
Challenge: learners find a published discussion text and analyse its stages.

blocks.x: Stage labels on a model (written for this book):

lines: Issue: Many cities are debating whether schools should start later in the morning.
Arguments for: Supporters argue that teenagers need more sleep…
Arguments against: On the other hand, parents who work early may find…
Recommendation: On balance, a modest change of thirty minutes may be the most practical solution.
S1: All three texts have a recommendation, but one puts it at the start as well.
T: So the order of the middle is flexible, but the stages are there. That’s a choice, not an error.

body: Purpose: to show analytical deconstruction. Content: a text shown as four coloured blocks lifted apart like building bricks, each labelled with its stage and with two or three language features written on it. Style: clean, exploded diagram. Board version: four boxes with labels and features.

items: Google Docs (free) with colour highlighting for stages.

blocks.x: Photocopies cut into stages for groups to reassemble.

pts: Teacher and learners collaboratively draft a text of the target genre, with the teacher modelling decision-making aloud.
This stage is often skipped in practice, but it's argued to be the crucial bridge between analysis and independent production.
It makes the largely invisible process of expert writing decisions visible and discussable.

v: The class chart from field-building; the board

items: Tell the class that together you will write a discussion text on the flyover topic.
Ask for an opening sentence. Write it on the board and think aloud about whether it states the issue clearly.
Continue sentence by sentence, asking learners for content and wording, and making decisions visible.
Refer back to the class chart of stages and features as you write.
Read the finished text aloud and ask learners what decisions they noticed.
In a large class, groups propose sentences on slips, and the teacher selects and discusses them.
Support: learners copy the joint text into their notebooks as a model.
Challenge: learners suggest an alternative sentence and argue for it.

lines: T: We have the issue. Now the arguments for. What’s our strongest point?
S1: Less traffic.
T: Good. How shall we start? ‘The flyover will reduce traffic’?
S2: But we don’t know it will. Maybe ‘could reduce’.
T: Excellent: that’s a hedge. We’re not certain, so ‘could’ is more honest. What evidence can we add?
S3: The traffic table. Four thousand vehicles an hour.
T: Where does that go, before or after the claim?

blocks.x: Joint construction is the stage most often skipped, yet it makes expert decisions visible and discussable (Martin and Rose 2008; Hyland 2007).

body: Purpose: to show joint construction. Content: a teacher writing on the board while speech bubbles from many learners offer words and ideas, with a thought bubble above the teacher reading ‘Is this clear to the reader?’. Style: lively classroom scene with benches. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free) projected, if a projector is available.

blocks.x: The blackboard, with the class chart displayed beside it.

body: In joint construction, think aloud about rejected options as well as chosen ones. Saying ‘I thought of “moreover” here, but the next point contrasts with the last one, so “however” is better’ teaches more than the final sentence alone.

pts: Learners produce their own genre example independently, drawing on the field-building, deconstruction and joint-construction stages.
This is the stage most writing instruction jumps to directly — the cycle argues that skipping ahead here is what fails many learners.
Feedback at this stage should reference the genre's specific moves and structure, not only sentence-level accuracy.

v: A new topic; a genre checklist

items: Give a new topic in the same genre, for example whether schools should serve millet-based meals.
Learners plan with the stage chart and do brief field-building of their own.
Learners draft independently.
The teacher holds short conferences with a few learners, referring to stages and features.
Learners check their drafts against the genre checklist before submitting.
Learners choose their own topic from a list, within the same genre.
Support: a planning frame with the four stages as headings.
Challenge: learners write for a real audience, such as the school magazine or a local newspaper.

blocks.x: A genre checklist (written for this book):

lines: Does the introduction state the issue and why it matters?
Are there arguments on both sides, each with evidence?
Are claims hedged where evidence is uncertain?
Does the recommendation follow from the arguments?
Are contrasts signalled clearly (however, on the other hand)?

blocks.x: Feedback at this stage refers to the genre’s stages and moves as well as to sentence-level accuracy.

pts: Run the full cycle for each new genre introduced across a course, rather than assuming it transfers automatically between genres.
This connects to Unit 11's unit-sequencing principles — a genre cycle maps naturally onto a multi-lesson unit structure.
Genre familiarity built this way transfers more reliably to genuinely novel texts of the same type.

v: The year’s syllabus or scheme of work

items: List the genres learners must write or speak during the year.
Group them into families, for example stories, reports, explanations and arguments.
Sequence the families so that each builds on the last.
Allocate a full cycle to each new genre, and shorter cycles to close variants.
Place the cycles in the scheme of work (Unit 14) as multi-lesson units (Unit 11).
Plan across grades with colleagues so that genres recur with increasing complexity.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

pts: Deconstruction-stage feedback addresses analytical accuracy; independent-construction feedback addresses genre production itself.
This connects to Unit 8's correction principles, applied with genre-stage-specific calibration.
Conflating these feedback types — correcting grammar during deconstruction, say — dilutes each stage's distinct purpose.

v: Samples of learner work from each stage

items: Collect a sample from each stage: a deconstruction worksheet, a contribution to joint construction and an independent draft.
For each, write the feedback you would normally give.
Check whether it matches the purpose of the stage.
Rewrite any feedback that addresses the wrong thing, such as grammar comments on a deconstruction worksheet.
Agree a simple stage-by-feedback grid with colleagues.
Share the grid with learners so they know what kind of feedback to expect at each stage.

lines: Building the field: Is the content accurate and sufficient?
Deconstruction: Has the learner identified stages and features correctly?
Joint construction: Were contributions relevant and well reasoned?
Independent construction: Does the text achieve its purpose through appropriate stages and language?

points.h: Adapting the Cycle for Speaking Genres
pts: The same four-stage cycle adapts well to spoken genres — a negotiation, a presentation, a formal complaint.
This connects directly to Unit 38's role-play and Unit 40's presentation-skills work, giving both a fuller pedagogical structure.
The joint-construction stage for speaking genres often takes the form of a modelled, teacher-led example interaction.

v: Two recorded or scripted complaint calls; role cards

items: Field: discuss a common problem, such as a mobile recharge that did not work.
Deconstruction: learners listen to or read two complaint calls and label the stages: greeting, problem, details, request, response, closing.
Joint construction: the teacher plays the caller and the class suggests each turn, while a learner plays the agent.
Independent construction: pairs role-play new complaints from cards.
Feedback on stages and politeness, using the language of Unit 53.
Apply the cycle to a presentation (Unit 40) or a negotiation (Unit 38).
Support: provide a stage frame with useful phrases.
Challenge: the agent can only offer a partial solution, so the caller must negotiate.

blocks.x: A modelled complaint (written for this book):

lines: A: Good morning, customer care. How can I help?
B: Good morning. I recharged my phone yesterday for ₹299, but the data pack hasn’t been activated.
A: I’m sorry about that. Could I have your number, please?
B: Yes, it’s… The transaction ID is on my screen too, if you need it.
A: Thank you. I can see the payment. I’ll activate the pack now. It should work within an hour.
B: Thank you. And if it doesn’t?
A: Please call again and quote this complaint number.

body: Choose one genre from next term’s syllabus and teach the full cycle, including at least one lesson of joint construction. Compare the independent texts with those from a class taught the genre in your usual way, noting the stages and language features each includes.

dek: Unit 54 of 100: a complete, well-evidenced cycle for moving learners from analysing a genre to producing it independently — Tier II's genre awareness, made fully operational.

aims.x: Many writing lessons follow the same pattern: read a model, discuss it briefly, then write your own. Confident learners manage. Many others produce a weaker copy of the model or a text that ignores it. This unit sets out a well-tested alternative, the teaching-learning cycle of genre-based pedagogy, which moves learners from understanding a topic, through analysing and jointly writing a text, to producing the genre independently. It turns the genre awareness of Unit 33 into a complete teaching procedure.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the four stages of the teaching-learning cycle and the principle of gradually reduced support;
plan field-building activities that give learners the content a genre needs;
lead a deconstruction stage that analyses stages, moves and language features across several models;
conduct joint construction, thinking aloud about the writer’s decisions;
support independent construction with genre-referenced criteria and conferencing;
plan a sequence of genre cycles across a course;
match feedback to the purpose of each stage;
adapt the cycle to spoken genres such as complaints and presentations.

why: Why this matters. Knowing a genre's structure (Tier II) is not the same as being able to produce it under one's own steam. This cycle is what bridges that specific gap.

background.x: Genre-based pedagogy in the Sydney School tradition grew out of work in Australian schools in the 1980s and 1990s. Linguists and teachers including J. R. Martin, Joan Rothery and later David Rose drew on systemic functional linguistics and on Vygotsky’s idea of learning with the support of a more expert other to design a cycle in which the teacher first makes the genre explicit and shares the writing, then hands control to learners (Rothery 1994). Beverly Derewianka’s Exploring How Texts Work (1990) brought these ideas to many classroom teachers.

The cycle has several versions. A common one has four stages: building the field (developing knowledge of the topic), deconstruction or modelling (analysing a model text), joint construction (teacher and class write a text together) and independent construction (learners write alone). Susan Feez (1998) developed a five-stage version for adult language programmes that adds linking to related texts. Ken Hyland (2004; 2007) has shown how genre pedagogy suits second language writers, because it makes explicit the expectations that native-speaker writers may acquire implicitly. It also fits the move analysis of John Swales (1990), introduced in Unit 33 and developed for academic writing in Unit 61.

Some critics have worried that explicit genre teaching could produce formulaic writing. Proponents reply that learners cannot vary a genre creatively until they control it, and that the cycle’s aim is conscious choice, not a template. In India, many learners meet writing as a set of memorized formats, such as the letter, notice and report of board examinations. The cycle keeps the clarity of formats while developing the thinking and reader awareness that memorization cannot supply. NCF 2023 describes writing as a process that develops through drafting and feedback (NCERT 2023), and the cycle provides a structure for exactly that. Home languages have a role too, especially in building the field: learners can research and discuss a local topic in Kannada, Telugu or Hindi before writing about it in English.

items: Deconstruction task. Learners label the stages and features of an unseen model and note one flexible choice.
Independent text. A text in the target genre, assessed with a rubric that includes stages, purpose and language features.
Genre checklist. Learners annotate their own draft against the checklist before submission.
Teacher plan. A genre map for the year with one fully planned cycle.
Which stage of the cycle do you most often skip, and why?
How much time do your learners spend writing alone without preparation?
How could you use learners’ home languages in building the field?
How do you think aloud when you write in front of a class?
Does your feedback match the purpose of each stage?
Which spoken genres would benefit from the same cycle?

terms.def: The first stage of the genre-based teaching-learning cycle, in which learners develop knowledge of the topic, for example by researching a local issue in Kannada or Hindi before writing about it in English.
In the genre-based teaching-learning cycle, the stage in which the teacher and learners analyse a model text to understand its purpose, structure and language; also called modelling.

An approach to teaching writing, and speaking, that makes the stages and language of genres explicit through a teaching-learning cycle of building the field, deconstruction, joint construction and independent construction. It is associated with the Sydney School.

A sequence in which responsibility moves step by step from teacher to learner: the teacher models, then learners work with support, then independently (Pearson and Gallagher 1983). It is often summarized as ‘I do, we do, you do’.
The stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which learners write a text of the genre on their own, after deconstruction and joint construction, using genre-referenced criteria.
A stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which teacher and class write a text together, with the teacher thinking aloud about the writer’s decisions.
In genre analysis, a stage of a text that performs a recognizable communicative function, such as ‘establishing a territory’ at the start of a research article introduction (Swales 1990).

In genre-based teaching, one of the typical functional steps through which a genre achieves its purpose, such as the orientation, complication and resolution of a narrative. Teachers analyse stages with learners before they write.

The genre-based approach developed in Australian schools from the 1980s by J. R. Martin, Joan Rothery, David Rose and colleagues, drawing on systemic functional linguistics to make powerful school genres explicit (Martin and Rose 2008).
The genre-based cycle of building the field, deconstructing model texts, joint construction and independent construction, with support gradually reduced (Martin and Rose 2008).
